zh.question: 如果云和空气一直在移动，台风的眼墙为什么还能保持？看不见风眼时，里面一定没有眼吗？
zh.observe: 先在成熟阶段转动三维云系，比较俯视、斜视与侧视；点持续观察，再用风场示踪和空气剖面追踪汇入、眼墙上升与高空外流。分别查看清晰风眼、没有清晰风眼和眼墙置换，最后从头看形成，并改变海温或风切变作对照。

academic.title: 同一个中心，眼内、眼墙和雨带各有不同
academic.body: 发展良好的强热带气旋可有少云、风较弱的眼，外围眼墙则集中了强风雨。为何强对流围成一圈，中心反而下沉？一种重要机制是，向内的角动量输送增强旋转，较高的惯性稳定度使继续径向进入更困难，边界层汇聚上升可集中在离中心一定半径处。眼墙凝结加热的径向差异促使气压、风场与次级环流调整，形成眼墙上升及内侧补偿下沉；下沉增温、降低相对湿度并增强稳定层结，进一步抑制中心深对流。摩擦和角动量交换也参与其中，不能只用“周围上升”断言中心必定下沉，更不是空气被甩空。眼墙并非实心墙，外雨带也不都属于眼墙。无清晰眼可能是尚未形成，或已有眼被高云遮住；本页演示前者。

academic.title: 准稳态保持形状，空气仍然运动
academic.body: 准稳态要在跟随风暴中心的参考系中理解：一段时间内平均风场和结构变化较慢，并不要求空气速度为零，也不等于风暴中心停止移动。暖海通过热量和水汽交换供能，凝结释放潜热，对流与环流相互维持；真实风暴仍会调整、增强或减弱。画面把形成进度与环流活动分开，只是为了持续观察结构。暖海并不保证生成，湿度、暖水深度和已有扰动也重要；强垂直风切变通常不利于上下环流对齐，却不是立即摧毁所有成熟气旋的开关。南北半球通常反向旋转，赤道附近则不利于通常的生成。生成期的飞机观测与高分辨率模拟支持对流单体反复新生、消散并与旋转环流相互加强，而不是同几朵云逐渐变成整个台风。对流伸展已有涡度、较大尺度汇入输送角动量，是其中的重要联系；不同风暴也可经历中心重组和对齐等不同路径。本演示用规定的气流输送同一云场，并加入局地生长与消散，保留过程连续性，但没有计算这些反馈，也不代表统一的必经阶段。

academic.title: 眼墙置换是一种结构重组，不是长出两个眼
academic.body: 部分强气旋的外围对流可组织成新的外眼墙，与原有内眼墙暂时共存，两者共用一个环流中心。中间常有对流和降雨较弱、下沉较明显的环状间隙，称为护城河区；它不是第二个风眼。随后内眼墙可能衰减，外眼墙收缩并接替它。外墙建立涉及低层汇入、对流组织和风场调整等过程，形成机制不止一种，研究仍在继续；并非任意雨带都会变成眼墙。置换可能扩大强风范围并改变最大风速，但不保证固定先弱后强，也不是每场台风的必经阶段。三维演示采用一种理想化顺序，不能据此推断真实时长或灾害减轻。

zh.misconception: 准稳态不是没有风，也不是风暴停在原地；没有清晰眼不等于没有危险，两圈眼墙更不是两只风眼。
zh.boundary: 三维云形、示踪点、雨区和剖面属于定性模型，云场输送中的气流与局地生消规则由人为给定，未求解真实风场、完整能量收支或云微物理。形成与置换时间经过压缩，场景选择不是天气分类或强度预报；不利条件下也不会因播放到终点而强制出现眼。现实中的风、雨与风暴潮风险以当地气象部门预警为准。

narration.label: 从上面看到侧面
narration.text: 我们先来看一场已经组织起来的大风暴。中间云比较少的地方，叫作眼。围着它的厚云环，叫作眼墙，那里常有很大的风和雨。外面弯弯的云带，也会下雨。把画面转一转，从上面看到侧面，再停一下，找找中心和高高的云环，它们是同一个地方吗？
narration.cue: 选择清晰风眼，使用俯视、斜视与侧视预设；最后保持斜视，留三秒观察，标注避开中心。

narration.label: 形状留下，空气在走
narration.text: 让风暴继续活动吧。形状大体还在，空气却没有停！空气向里走时往往转得更快，不会全挤到正中，许多暖湿空气在周围升高，形成眼墙。云滴形成时放出的热，也让整团气流一起调整，中心一些空气反而慢慢下降。空气下沉变暖，云就不容易留下，这能帮助形成眼。还有空气从高处向外散开。温暖海水继续送来热量和水汽，帮助这些活动维持。
narration.cue: 点持续观察；风场示踪显示运动后，切空气剖面，依次强调近海面汇入、眼墙上升、高空外流与眼内缓慢下沉。

narration.label: 风眼为什么不见了
narration.text: 换一种结构看看：这回，中心被云占着，还没有形成清晰的眼。有时，真正的风暴已经有眼，却被上面的云遮住了，所以，看不见可能有不同原因。再把高处和低处的风差调大一些，云团可能更难聚拢。暖海水很有帮助，却不能保证一定长出漂亮的风眼。
narration.cue: 切没有清晰风眼，停留比较中心对流；保持海温，增大风切变。讲到高云遮蔽时不把当前场景误标为已有眼。

narration.label: 一圈眼墙接替另一圈
narration.text: 最后看一种特别变化。原来的眼墙外面，又有一圈眼墙慢慢形成。两圈之间，雨比较少。后来，里面那圈变弱，外面那圈向里收，接过了它的位置。这叫眼墙置换，可不是长出了两个眼，也不是每场台风都会这样。再从头看：云随风移动，也不断长出和散去，慢慢组织起来，不是同几朵云一直转到最后。真正遇到台风，还是要和大人听天气预警。
narration.cue: 恢复有利条件，选眼墙置换，分别停在外墙建立、双墙间隙、内墙衰减与外墙收缩；结束后切回清晰眼并从头看形成。形成阶段停在早、中、后段，比较云的位置、拉长和局部新生，不把它讲成几朵云的永久聚合。

en.question: If clouds and air keep moving, how can an eyewall persist? Does an eye that cannot be seen always mean there is no eye?
en.observe: Start at maturity and rotate the three-dimensional clouds, comparing overhead, oblique and side views. Start continuous observation, then follow inflow, eyewall ascent and upper outflow in the wind-tracer and air-cross-section views. Compare a clear eye, no clear eye and eyewall replacement. Finally, watch formation from the beginning and compare sea-temperature or wind-shear settings.

academic.title: One center, different motions in the eye, eyewall and rainbands
academic.body: A well-developed strong tropical cyclone can have a clearer, calmer eye surrounded by an eyewall of strong winds and heavy rain. Why does deep convection form a ring while the center subsides? In one important mechanism, inward angular-momentum transport strengthens rotation, and higher inertial stability makes further radial displacement harder. Boundary-layer convergence and ascent can concentrate at a finite radius. Radial differences in eyewall condensation heating make pressure, winds and the secondary circulation adjust, supporting eyewall ascent and compensating descent on its inner side. Descent warms the air, lowers relative humidity and increases static stability, further suppressing central deep convection. Friction and angular-momentum exchange also contribute. Surrounding ascent alone does not prove that descent must occur at the center, and air is not flung out to leave a vacuum. The eyewall is not a solid wall, and outer rainbands are not all eyewalls. An unclear eye may be undeveloped or hidden by high clouds; this page illustrates the former.

academic.title: A quasi-steady structure still contains moving air
academic.body: Quasi-steady is understood in a reference frame following the storm center: its average wind field and structure change relatively slowly over an interval. Air velocity need not be zero, and the storm center need not stop moving. Ocean heat and moisture exchange supplies energy; condensation releases latent heat, and convection interacts with the circulation. Real storms still adjust, intensify or weaken. Separating formation progress from circulating motion is a teaching choice that lets us keep observing the structure. Warm water alone does not guarantee formation: humidity, warm-water depth and an existing disturbance matter. Strong vertical shear generally hinders an aligned circulation but does not instantly destroy every mature cyclone. Rotation usually reverses between hemispheres, while conditions near the equator hinder the usual formation process. Aircraft observations and high-resolution simulations of genesis support recurring convective-cell growth and decay interacting with an evolving rotating circulation, rather than the same clouds becoming an entire cyclone. Stretching of existing vorticity by convection and inward angular-momentum transport by larger-scale inflow are important links. Storms can also follow different paths involving center reorganization and alignment. Here prescribed winds transport one cloud field with local growth and evaporation, preserving continuity without solving these feedbacks or imposing a universal sequence of necessary stages.

academic.title: Eyewall replacement reorganizes the storm; it does not create two eyes
academic.body: In some strong cyclones, outer convection organizes into a new outer eyewall that temporarily coexists with the original inner wall around one circulation center. The separating ring often has weaker convection, lighter rain and more pronounced descent. Called a moat, it is not a second eye. The inner wall may then decay as the outer wall contracts and replaces it. Low-level inflow, convective organization and wind-field adjustments can all contribute; there is no single formation mechanism, and research continues. Not every rainband becomes an eyewall. Replacement can broaden the strong-wind region and change peak winds, but does not guarantee weakening followed by strengthening or occur in every typhoon. This demonstration uses one idealized sequence; it does not predict real timing or reduced hazards.

en.misconception: Quasi-steady does not mean windless or stationary over one place. No clear eye does not mean no danger, and two eyewalls are not two eyes.
en.boundary: Three-dimensional clouds, tracers, rain regions and the cross-section are qualitative models, with prescribed advection and local source/sink rules, without a solved physical wind field, full energy budget or cloud microphysics. Formation and replacement time are compressed. Scene choices are not weather classifications or intensity forecasts, and reaching the end under unfavorable conditions does not force an eye to appear. Follow local weather warnings for wind, rain and storm-surge risks.

narration.label: From above to the side
narration.text: Let us begin with a big storm that has already organized. The center with fewer clouds is called the eye. The thick cloud ring around it is the eyewall, where winds and rain are often very strong. The curved cloud bands farther out bring rain too. Turn the picture from above to the side. Pause and find the center and the tall cloud ring. Are they the same place?
narration.cue: Choose the clear-eye scene and use overhead, oblique and side presets. Hold the oblique view for three seconds; keep labels away from the center.

narration.label: The shape stays while air moves
narration.text: Let the storm keep moving. Its overall shape stays, but the air has not stopped! Air moving inward often spins faster instead of all crowding into the very center. Much of the warm, moist air rises around it, forming the eyewall. Heat released as cloud droplets form also makes the whole circulation adjust, and some air in the center slowly sinks instead. Sinking air warms, making it harder for clouds to remain. This helps an eye form. Other air spreads outward high above. Warm seawater keeps supplying heat and water vapor to help these movements continue.
narration.cue: Start continuous observation. Show motion with wind tracers, then switch to the air cross-section and emphasize near-surface inflow, eyewall ascent, upper outflow and slow eye descent in turn.

narration.label: Where did the eye go?
narration.text: Try a different structure. This time, clouds fill the center and a clear eye has not formed. Sometimes a real storm already has an eye, but clouds high above hide it. So not seeing an eye can have different causes. Now make the winds high above more different from those below. The clouds may find it harder to stay organized. Warm seawater helps, but it cannot promise a clear, neat eye.
narration.cue: Choose no clear eye and compare central convection. Hold temperature fixed and increase shear. When discussing high-cloud obscuration, do not label this scene as an existing hidden eye.

narration.label: One eyewall replaces another
narration.text: Now watch a special change. A new eyewall gradually forms outside the old one. There is less rain between the two rings. Later, the inner ring weakens while the outer ring draws inward and takes its place. This is called eyewall replacement. It does not make two eyes, and not every typhoon does it. Replay formation: clouds move with the wind, but new clouds also grow as others fade away. They gradually organize; the first few clouds do not survive the whole process. With a real typhoon, listen to weather warnings with an adult.
narration.cue: Restore favorable conditions and choose eyewall replacement. Pause at outer-wall formation, the two walls and their gap, inner-wall decay, and outer-wall contraction. Then return to a clear eye and restart formation. During formation, compare early, middle and late cloud positions, stretching and local growth; do not describe permanent merging of the original clouds.
